Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Meera

Meera was sixty-six years old when she first came to the clinic, though the therapist noted she moved with the careful deliberation of someone much older, as though her body had learned not to trust sudden motion. She had been widowed for twelve years and worked part-time at a department store in Queens, folding sweaters and helping customers find their sizes—work she had held onto with a quiet desperation, though it had become increasingly difficult to sustain.

The assault had happened forty-three years earlier, when Meera was twenty-three. She had been a young bride then, newly arrived from Gujarat, living with her husband's family in a cramped apartment in Jackson Heights. One afternoon, while her mother-in-law was at the market and her husband at work, a man who had been doing repairs on the building had forced his way inside. He had smelled of cigarette smoke and sweat. The violence had lasted perhaps twenty minutes, though Meera's memory of it existed not as a continuous narrative but as a series of frozen frames: his face above hers, his hand over her mouth, the way the afternoon light had sliced through the bedroom window in a particular angle, the sound of her own breathing, the smell—that acrid, suffocating smell of smoke that seemed to penetrate everything.

For decades, Meera had told no one. She had cleaned herself, changed her clothes, and said nothing when her husband came home. The trauma had lived inside her like a stone she carried in silence, and over the years she had learned, or believed she had learned, to live with it. But three years ago, something had shifted. She had been working a Saturday shift when a customer—a man in his sixties—had approached her while she was alone in the back storage room. He had not done anything threatening; he had simply asked her for help finding a particular brand of shirt. But he had closed the door behind him, and in that moment, with no one else nearby, Meera's entire body had seized with a terror so complete that she had not been able to speak. She had pointed mutely toward the shelves and waited for him to leave. Since then, she had not been able to be alone with any man without her heart racing, without the conviction that something terrible was about to happen.

The smell of smoke had become similarly inescapable. The store's café area, just visible from where she worked, sometimes produced a burnt smell from the espresso machine, and on those days, Meera found herself unable to concentrate, her mind flooded with fragments of memory so vivid and immediate that she would have to excuse herself to the bathroom. She had come to believe that the world was filled with people who behaved without conscience—the man who had assaulted her had never been found, never been held accountable—and she saw evidence of this moral chaos everywhere. When she witnessed customers being rude to staff, or heard about news stories of violence, she felt a kind of despair settle over her, a confirmation that the world was fundamentally unsafe and unjust.

Over the past two years, she had begun to withdraw. Her daughter had invited her to family dinners, but Meera had made excuses. Her son-in-law would be there, and the thought of sitting across from him at a table, of being in a room where she could not easily leave, had become unbearable. She had stopped attending her temple. She had reduced her hours at the store, claiming back pain, though the real pain was something more diffuse—a sense that nothing she did mattered anymore, that her life had been hollowed out by what had happened so long ago, and that no amount of time or effort could restore meaning to it.

What had finally brought her to the clinic was a moment of unexpected clarity. Her granddaughter, now twelve, had asked her why she never came to visit anymore, why she seemed so sad all the time. Meera had looked at the girl's face and realized that she was passing something down, some invisible weight, and that terrified her more than anything else. She was not sure therapy could help—she was not sure anything could undo what had been done—but she had made the appointment, and she had come.
